# Volatile

In Java, threads are not automatically guaranteed to observe each other’s
updates to shared variables. Values used while a thread executes may be held
transiently in registers or CPU caches, and compiled code may reuse a value it
has already read rather than perform another memory read. As a result, if one
thread updates a shared field such as `boolean ready`, another thread may
continue to observe an earlier value indefinitely.

Consider a shared object with a field: `boolean ready`, initially set to false.

```
Abstract observation model — not a physical storage diagram

Value used by Thread 1                     Shared object field
+----------------------+                   +----------------------+
| ready: false         |                   | ready: false         |
+----------------------+                   +----------------------+
```

Values used while a thread executes may be held transiently in registers or CPU
caches, and compiled code may reuse a value it has already read rather than
perform another memory read. Therefore, after another thread later changes the
field, a thread may continue using an earlier observed value.

Thread 2 reads the shared object’s `ready` field and observes `false`, as
illustrated below.

```
Abstract observation model — not a physical storage diagram

Value used by Thread 1                     Shared object field
+----------------------+                   +----------------------+
| ready: false         |                   | ready: false         |
+----------------------+                   +-+--------------------+
                                             |
Value used by Thread 2                       |
+----------------------+                     |
| ready: false  <------+- reads -------------+
+----------------------+
```

Thread 1 later writes `true` to `ready`. Because the program has not established
an ordering relationship between that write and Thread 2’s reads, Thread 2 is
not guaranteed to observe `true`; it may continue to observe `false`.

```
Abstract observation model — not a physical storage diagram

Value used by Thread 1                     Shared object field
+----------------------+                   +----------------------+
| ready: true  --------+- writes ----------+-> ready: true        |
+----------------------+                   +----------------------+

Stale value used by Thread 2
+----------------------+
| ready: false         |
+----------------------+
```

Under the Java Memory Model (JMM), declaring `ready` as `volatile` makes its
reads and writes synchronization actions. A write to `ready` happens-before
every subsequent read of `ready`. Therefore, after Thread 1 writes `true`, a
subsequent read of `ready` by Thread 2 observes `true`, provided no later write
changes the field.

```
Abstract observation model — not a physical storage diagram

Value used by Thread 1                     Shared object field
+----------------------+                   +----------------------+
| ready: true  --------+- writes ----------+-> ready: true        |
+----------------------+                   +-+--------------------+
                                             |
Value observed by Thread 2                   |
after a volatile read                        |
+----------------------+                     |
| ready: true   <------+- reads -------------+
+----------------------+
```

`volatile` also establishes an ordering relationship. When a thread writes
shared state and then writes to a `volatile` field, that volatile write
happens-before a subsequent read of the same field by another thread.
Consequently, after that read, the other thread can observe the effects of the
earlier writes.

`volatile` does not make compound operations such as `counter++` atomic and does
not provide mutual exclusion.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this example, attendees can:

- explain the JMM’s role in determining which shared writes a thread can
  observe;
- explain the happens-before edge created by a volatile write and read;
- use that edge to safely publish an earlier ordinary-field write; and
- distinguish visibility and ordering from mutual exclusion and atomicity.

## Prerequisite

Install a
[Oracle Java 8](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java8) JDK
or newer to compile and run this example. Ensure `java` and `javac` resolve to
Java 8 or newer in the terminal you use for the workshop.

## The program to inspect

Consider the following example

```java
package demo;

import static java.util.Objects.requireNonNull;

public final class Publication {

    private String message;
    private volatile boolean ready;

    public void publish(final String message) {
        this.message = requireNonNull(message, "The message cannot be null");
        ready = true;
    }

    public String awaitMessage() {
        while (!ready) {
            // Wait until the volatile read observes the publisher's volatile write.
        }

        return message;
    }
}
```

`message` is deliberately an ordinary field. It is safe here because the write
to it comes before the volatile write in the publisher, and the reader’s
successful volatile read comes before its ordinary read of `message`.

The full happens-before path is:

```text
publisher: write message
    → program order → write volatile ready = true
    → synchronizes-with → reader observes ready == true
    → program order → reader: read message
```

The volatile write and read create the synchronizes-with edge; happens-before is
the transitive closure of that edge and each thread’s program order. Thus, the
reader can safely observe the ordinary `message` write after it has observed
`ready == true`. This guarantees visibility and ordering only; it does not make
later updates to `message` safe or turn several actions into one atomic action.

The loop within the `awaitMessage()` method is not an example of efficient
waiting: it consumes a CPU while it is waiting. Its narrow purpose is to expose
the volatile read. Do not infer any happens-before relationship from the loop
itself, its timing, output, or a particular JVM implementation.

`volatile` does not make a compound action atomic and does not provide mutual
exclusion. For example, `if (!ready) { ready = true; }` is still a non-atomic
check-then-act sequence. Use a lock or an atomic compare-and-set operation when
an invariant requires an atomic state transition.

This is a one-shot publication protocol: one publisher changes `ready` from
`false` to `true`, and readers can then observe the published message. It is not
a resettable or multi-update protocol.

## When not to use `volatile`

Do not use `volatile` when correctness depends on an atomic read-modify-write
operation or an invariant spanning multiple fields. It cannot make several
writes appear as one state transition.

Do not use it for efficient waiting or work signalling. The loop in this
example deliberately spins to expose the volatile read; production code should
use a coordination mechanism with the required blocking and lifecycle contract.

`volatile` is not a substitute for mutual exclusion, a queue, or a cancellation
protocol. Choose a lock, an atomic operation, or a coordination utility when
the operation requires the corresponding guarantee.

## Guided walkthrough

Run these commands from this example directory. Choose one of the following
ways to run the example.

1. Run the example using the
   [Maven `exec` plugin](https://www.mojohaus.org/exec-maven-plugin/).

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean compile exec:exec
   ```

   One possible trace. The ordering of messages from different threads varies.

   ```
   ...
   [12:34:56.789] [                                             Thread[main,5,main]] Starting the reader thread
   [12:34:56.792] [                                             Thread[main,5,main]] Giving the reader time to enter awaitMessage()
   [12:34:56.792] [                                           Thread[READER,5,main]] Fetching the publication message
   [12:34:57.292] [                                             Thread[main,5,main]] Publishing the message
   [12:34:57.292] [                                             Thread[main,5,main]] Waiting for the reader to complete
   [12:34:57.292] [                                           Thread[READER,5,main]] Reader observed: published before ready
   [12:34:57.292] [                                             Thread[main,5,main]] Done
   ...
   ```

   The reader prints the complete message after its volatile read observes
   `true`. That volatile happens-before relationship guarantees visibility of
   the earlier message write. The output is an illustration, not evidence based
   on thread scheduling or timing.

2. Build the application and create the JAR file.

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean package
   ```

   (*Optional*) List the created JAR file.

   ```shell
   tree --dirsfirst --sort=name './target/libs'
   ```

   The application JAR file

   ```
   ./target/libs
   └── volatile-1.0.0.jar

   1 directory, 1 file
   ```

   Run the application.

   ```shell
   java \
     -classpath './target/libs/*' \
     demo.Main
   ```

   One possible run; thread ordering will vary.

   ```
   [12:34:59.928] [                                             Thread[main,5,main]] Starting the reader thread
   [12:34:59.930] [                                             Thread[main,5,main]] Giving the reader time to enter awaitMessage()
   [12:34:59.931] [                                           Thread[READER,5,main]] Fetching the publication message
   [12:35:00.431] [                                             Thread[main,5,main]] Publishing the message
   [12:35:00.431] [                                             Thread[main,5,main]] Waiting for the reader to complete
   [12:35:00.431] [                                           Thread[READER,5,main]] Reader observed: published before ready
   [12:35:00.431] [                                             Thread[main,5,main]] Done
   ```
